To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bioavailability of sediment-associated chemicals is best described by the desorbing fraction or pore-water concentrations.

the desorbing fraction of sediment‐dissolved organic matter–associated PCB 77 and pore‐water PCB concentrations predicted the bioavailability in sediment‐exposed oligochaetes better than the standard equilibrium partition model, and that the bioavailable fraction was modified by the sediment ingested by the oligochaetes.
the bioavailable fraction is a dynamic process and that sediment ingestion by oligochaetes increases the bioavailability of PCB 77.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the assessment of bioavailable fractions of chemicals in sediments and the role of sediment ingestion in the bioaccumulation of contaminants.
the influence of the chemical concentration in sediment and the sediment‐ingestion behavior on the desorption and bioavailable fractions of sediment‐associated contaminants in benthic invertebrates.
the influence of sediment ingestion and concentration on the bioavailability of PCB 77.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

pore‐water concentrations or the desorbing fractions are more precise than equilibrium partitioning in predicting the bioavailable fraction, but that feeding can increase the bioavailable fraction in oligochaetes.
bioavailability of sediment‐associated contaminants is a complex phenomenon and cannot be described by simple equilibrium partition models.
the bioavailability of sediment‐associated PCB 77 is a complex function that depends on the exposure concentration, the chemical characteristics, and the feeding behavior of the organism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pore‐water concentrations and desorbing fractions can provide more accurate bioavailable fractions of sediment‐associated chemicals than the standard equilibrium partition model.

the bioavailable fraction is not only a function of the sediment concentration, but is also dependent on the exposure concentration, and that the bioavailable fractions are not always in equilibrium with pore‐water concentrations.

the bioavailability of sediment‐associated chemicals can be estimated with more precision if desorption kinetics are considered, but that sediment ingestion may be an important factor in the bioavailability of some sediment‐associated chemicals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bioavailability is not a constant fraction of sediment concentration and can vary considerably depending on exposure conditions.
sediment‐ingestors have access to an additional fraction of sediment‐bound chemical that is bioavailable.
sediment‐associated chemicals may be bioavailable to sediment‐inhabiting organisms in different forms than previously assumed.
